A wide variety of materials have been and continue to be used to build the roofs of houses. In modern residential construction, asphalt composite shingles are the most popular roofing material in North America, made from a fiberglass base topped with asphalt and mineral granules, and typically lasting 12–30 years [d1][d6]. Metal roofing—including steel, aluminum, copper, and zinc—is also widely used, with steel being the most common metal option due to its durability, while aluminum is favored for its lightweight properties [d5][d2]. Other common modern materials include clay and concrete tiles (well-suited for hot climates), rubber/EPDM membranes (used primarily on flat or low-slope roofs), wood shingles and shakes, and built-up roofing (BUR) systems made of layered asphalt-impregnated felt and crushed stone [d1][d3][d6]. Historically, roofing materials have been far more varied: ancient and medieval houses used thatched roofs, clay tiles, wood shingles, slate tiles, marble, and Portland cement, while regional traditions included palm-leaf mats over wooden beams, dried mud with reeds and leaves, oak shingles, and earth mixed with straw [d7][d8].
